note:
Researched from live web sources in a Claude Code session — no paid API, no key, no cost.

`case` is the argument for picking them; `watch_out` is the honest counter-argument, because a recommendation you can't argue against isn't advice. `key_stats` holds the hard numbers as discrete facts. `voices` records what named outlets actually said — 'analysts say' is not a source. `dissent` marks a genuine split.

REWRITTEN for GW2 after a specific failure: the model dropped Haaland on the back of a single blank. Every entry below is now weighted against multi-season evidence rather than one weekend, and the cases lead with what people are actually saying and why, not with a projection. A GW1 haul is treated as thin evidence unless something structural sits behind it; a GW1 blank from a proven asset is treated as noise.

Club-wide verdicts do NOT belong here; they live in teams.json.

players.name: De Cuyper
players.verdict: The most-bought player in the game, and for once the bandwagon has a structural reason behind it.
players.case: He was the highest-scoring player of Gameweek 1 on 17 points — four shots, three key passes, a goal and an assist — and his 1.68 expected goal involvements was the highest of any player in the round, not just any Brighton player. The reason that isn't simply a one-week spike is positional: he played as a left winger rather than a full-back, and with Minteh expected to be out for around two months there is a good chance he keeps the advanced role. That gives him a midfielder's attacking upside while FPL still classifies him as a defender, which is the single most valuable mispricing available in this game.
players.watch_out: The whole case rests on a role that has been seen once. If Minteh returns early, or Brighton revert him to left-back, what remains is a full-back at an inflated price with none of the upside being paid for. Nearly 250,000 managers have already bought him, so the differential value is gone too — you are buying at the top of the bandwagon.
key_stats: 17 points in GW1 — the highest score of any player
1.68 xGI in GW1 — the highest of any player in the round
4 shots and 3 key passes from a defender-classified player
Played left wing, not left-back; Minteh out roughly two months
~250,000 transfers in ahead of GW2 — the most-bought player in the game

voices.take: Call him a perfectly reasonable transfer if you didn't start with him, and single out the positional change rather than the 17 points as the real reason.
Ran a dedicated buy-keep-or-sell piece on him ahead of GW2, which is itself a signal of how much of the community is weighing this move.

players.name: Calafiori
players.verdict: Delivered exactly what the pre-season case said he would, and the fixtures haven't turned yet.
players.case: He continued his Community Shield form into the opening weekend with an assist and a clean sheet, which is the specific combination that makes an attacking defender worth owning — the floor and the ceiling arriving in the same afternoon. He is one of three Arsenal players among the eight most-bought ahead of GW2, alongside Odegaard and Tzolis, so the market has moved to the same conclusion. Arsenal's opening run remains the softest in the league.
players.watch_out: Arsenal's defensive rotation is still unsettled with first-choice centre-backs working back to fitness, and Calafiori is the one whose place is least assured when everyone is available. He was a differential a week ago and isn't now, so you are paying a higher price for a place in the side that is no more certain than it was.

players.name: Haaland
players.verdict: The single biggest mistake available this week is selling him on one blank. Every outlet covering GW2 says the same thing, and the historical record is emphatic.
players.case: He blanked in GW1 — five shots, two on target, and a first-half chance he missed the ball on entirely in City's 2-1 win at Bournemouth. That is the whole of the bear case, and it is one match. Set against it: he has been the top-scoring player in the game after the first six gameweeks in ALL FOUR of his seasons at Manchester City, averaging nine goals and 61.3 points across that opening window each time. Last season he ranked first in the entire league for goals (27), shots (126), shots on target (59), expected goals (27.68) AND big chances (51) — not first among strikers, first outright, in all five. He won the Golden Boot for the third time in four attempts and finished as the top-scoring outfield player in FPL on 239 points. The season before that, a December slump and a spring injury held him to 22 goals and 181 points, and that is his floor — a bad Haaland season is still a very good FPL forward. Opta's verdict is that going without him is a brave call at any point, and that the start of a season is when it carries the most risk of all. City then have four home games in the first seven gameweeks, two of them against promoted Coventry and Ipswich, which is where most managers are planning their first Triple Captain.
players.watch_out: He is £15.5m — a record price — and that is a genuine structural cost, not a detail. Roughly a sixth of your entire budget sits in one player, and it is the reason a squad built around him has to be thinner everywhere else. The 24/25 season is the honest warning: 10 goals in his first six games, then three in the following thirteen as City fell away, and an injury in the spring. He is not immune to a slump. And at 71% ownership he buys you no rank when he hauls — he only protects you from losing rank when he does. GW2 is away at Crystal Palace, a genuinely awkward fixture, and Bournemouth was the first time in five seasons he has failed to score in City's opening game.
key_stats: Top-scoring player in the game after the first 6 GWs in all 4 of his seasons at City
Averages 9 goals and 61.3 points across those opening six-gameweek windows
2025/26: 27 goals — and ranked 1st in the league for shots (126), shots on target (59), xG (27.68) and big chances (51)
2025/26: 239 FPL points, the top-scoring outfield player; 3rd Golden Boot in 4 seasons
2024/25 (his worst season): 22 goals, 3 assists, 181 points from 31 games
GW1 2026/27: 5 shots, 2 on target, no goal — his first ever blank in a City league opener
£15.5m, a record FPL price; 71% owned
City have 4 home games in the first 7 GWs, including promoted Coventry and Ipswich

voices.take: Going without Haaland is a brave choice at any stage of the season, and the data says the start of a campaign is when that decision carries the most risk.
Names Haaland the safer captain for GW2, with João Pedro, Mbeumo and Bruno Fernandes as the aggressive alternatives — i.e. he is the baseline you deviate from, not a pick you have to justify.
Covered the GW1 blank explicitly in its notes and did not move him off the must-have list; flagged that he still generated five shots.
Listed him among the must-haves for the season start: 'his history shows it'll be a major risk to go without him in your opening squad'.
Haaland's goal threat remains significant for the trip to Crystal Palace despite failing to score against Bournemouth.

dissent.case: At roughly 71% ownership his haul barely moves your rank and his blank barely hurts it — owning and captaining him is tracking the field rather than beating it. After a blanking opening weekend a meaningful minority are arguing the £15.5m is better spread across two players with better GW2 fixtures. Note what this argument is NOT: nobody in it is claiming he won't score. It is an argument about effective ownership and opportunity cost, which is what the rank-strategy control is for — it does not damp his projection.

players.name: B.Fernandes
players.verdict: Among the most-sold in the game — and the projection models' preferred captain for this gameweek. Those two facts are the story.
players.case: Manchester United host newly-promoted Ipswich, and lead the entire league on clean-sheet probability this week at 48% — the only side above 40% other than Coventry. RotoWire's model has him tied for the top overall score in the gameweek and names him the preferred captain. He remains on penalties, corners and direct free-kicks, and produced 9 goals and a record 24 assists last season. The crowd is selling him off one bad afternoon into the best home fixture on the board.
players.watch_out: United flopped in GW1 and he is among the most-sold players in the game as a result, so this is a hold that will feel worse before it feels better. The pre-season penalty misses that Fantasy Football Scout flagged remain unresolved, and his case leans on dead balls more than most.

voices.take: Head their GW2 midfield rankings with him as the preferred captain, with the model tying him for the top overall score on a home date against a promoted side.
List him among the most-sold players ahead of Gameweek 2 following Manchester United's poor opening result, and separately rate Man Utd the best clean-sheet bet of the week at 48%.
Frame selling a premium the week before the fixture he was bought for as the archetypal post-GW1 kneejerk.

dissent.case: Worth being explicit that the crowd and the models are pointing opposite ways here. He is one of the most-sold players in the game after Manchester United flopped in GW1, and a large number of managers have concluded the side is the problem rather than the fixture. The models disagree and have him as the week's preferred captain. This app follows the models on this one — a home tie against a promoted side with the league's best clean-sheet odds is a fixture, and a fixture is a better basis for one week than a mood is — but it is a genuine split, not a settled call.

players.name: Sangare
players.verdict: The week's second bandwagon, off a haul against Spurs.
players.case: He hauled in the opening weekend against a Tottenham side that was comprehensively beaten, and has attracted almost 200,000 new owners as a result. At his price he is the kind of budget enabler that makes a premium-heavy structure affordable, which is the job most managers are actually trying to fill this week.
players.watch_out: One haul against a team having a bad day is the thinnest evidence in this file. Nothing about the underlying numbers has been established, and the entire ownership move is built on a single afternoon — the exact pattern AllAboutFPL are warning against this week.

players.name: Palmer
players.verdict: Right player, wrong week — Chelsea meet the defence that gave up nothing in GW1.
players.case: Chelsea were excellent against Fulham on the opening weekend and he is the focal point of that attack.
players.watch_out: Brighton are the opponent, and they are a different proposition to Fulham: among the best defences in the league last season, and they allowed their GW1 opponents zero shots on target. Analysts are explicitly saying to think twice about buying Chelsea attackers into this fixture. Buying an attacker for one week against a defence in that form is paying full price for the worst version of him.

players.name: Joao Pedro
players.verdict: Same fixture problem as Palmer, and he is far more widely owned.
players.case: He led the line in a Chelsea side that opened the season by taking Fulham apart, and arrived fresher than almost anyone after missing the World Cup.
players.watch_out: Brighton in GW2 is the issue: zero shots on target conceded in the opening weekend and one of the meanest defensive records in the league last season. At around 44% ownership the downside is shared with much of the field, which softens the rank damage but does nothing for your actual score. This is a hold-and-wait rather than a buy.

players.name: Szoboszlai
players.verdict: The set-piece and penalty route into a Liverpool side back at Anfield — bought for the role, not for last week's points.
players.case: He scored Liverpool's stoppage-time penalty against Newcastle in GW1, which matters far less than the reason he was on it: he is involved in corners and free-kicks and is taking spot-kicks. Set-piece and penalty duty is the most persistent, least fixture-dependent source of FPL points there is — it survives bad form, bad matchups and tactical changes in a way that open-play output does not. Liverpool now return to Anfield to face Nottingham Forest. Multiple outlets have him as one of the strongest value picks in the game right now.
players.watch_out: Penalty duty at Liverpool has moved around before, and one converted spot-kick is not a confirmed long-term appointment — watch who takes the next one. His open-play returns have historically been modest for a midfielder at his price, so if the penalties dry up the underlying case thins out fast.

players.name: Kayode
players.verdict: A £4.5m defender with a winger's shot count — the cheapest real differential on the board.
players.case: Four shots in GW1 from a defender, and the fourth-best xGI of ANY defender in the round. At £4.5m and 6.5% ownership he is the definition of what a differential should be: low-owned with a credible route to points, rather than low-owned because nobody wants him. The 2025/26 defensive contributions rule makes cheap attacking full-backs materially better than they used to be — 10 clearances, blocks, interceptions and tackles is worth 2 points on its own, before any clean sheet.
players.watch_out: One gameweek of shot volume from a full-back is exactly the kind of thing that regresses hard. Brentford are not a side you would bank clean sheets on, and at £4.5m he is priced as a bench defender for a reason. If the shots stop, there is very little underneath.

players.name: Wissa
players.verdict: The differential the community keeps pointing at: form, underlying numbers, fixture and 2.8% ownership all lining up at once.
players.case: Described as the perfect combination of form, underlying numbers, fixture and differential potential. That combination is rare — most 3%-owned players are cheap for a reason. The broader 25/26 lesson applies directly here: mid-price forwards outscored every premium midfielder bar Bruno Fernandes last season, and the £7-8m forward bracket is now the strongest position group in the game.
players.watch_out: Very low ownership means very little consensus support — you are early, or you are wrong, and there is no crowd to be wrong with. Brentford's attacking output has historically been volatile week to week.

voices.take: At just 2.8% ownership, Wissa gives you the perfect combination of form, underlying numbers, fixture and differential potential.

players.name: Mbeumo
players.verdict: Home to Ipswich with a two-season record that says the GW1 defeat was about Manchester United, not about him.
players.case: He finished second in the entire game on 236 points in 2024/25 — an improvement of 109 points on the season before — and was the top midfielder for expected goals in 2025/26. That is two consecutive seasons of elite underlying output, which is a very different thing from a player having one good week. Manchester United host Ipswich at Old Trafford in GW2, and a promoted side adjusting to the top flight is the softest fixture profile available. Multiple outlets flag him as a high-ceiling captaincy differential for anyone wanting to move off Haaland.
players.watch_out: United lost 2-0 at home to promoted Hull in GW1, which is the kind of result that makes 'they're at home to Ipswich' a much less comfortable sentence than it looks. The attacking returns have to survive a team playing badly, and last week they did not.
